newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Starbucks coffee shops push ahead in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Starbucks coffee shops push ahead in Asia.

text.p: U.S. coffee firm Starbucks Corp.'s expansion into Asia is ahead of forecasts and there is still space for robust growth in its key home market, the president of Starbucks Coffee International said Thursday.
"We've now got three stores in Tokyo and their sales are all about 25 percent above our plan," Howard Behar said in an interview ahead of the opening of Starbucks' first shop in Singapore.
He said the company expected to have 15 coffee shops in Japan and 10 in Singapore by next September.
Behar said Starbucks' move into Asia did not mean that its U.S. market, where the Seattle-based company has experienced sales growth of between 40 percent to 50 percent a year, was saturated.
"We have about 1,050 stores in the States and there's still plenty of opportunity," he said, adding that Starbucks plans to open a total of 325 shops in the 1997 fiscal year.
"We don't need to go to the markets. We have $200 million in cash. That's plenty of reserves to fund our growth," he said.
Behar said he had heard that Starbucks' peak Christmas sales in the United States were "holding up well."

Starbucks will have invested $10 million in developing its Asian operations by the end of the year, with the figure rising to $20 million if the contribution of its joint venture partners in the region are taken into account, Behar said.
He said he expected the companies' Asian coffee shops to make a "significant contribution" to the company's earnings in less than five years.

Behar said coffee was not traditionally a big part of Asian culture but that this was changing and Starbucks had partly selected Singapore for its first shop in the region because it was the most "Westernized" of the area's cities.
But he said the most crucial part of selecting new locations was the existence of a reliable local partner and said it would be a key factor in determining future sites.
Behar said the company had evaluated the European market, but felt that Asia offered more potential, though it would consider Europe again after it was successful in the Far East.
The company purchases around 70 million pounds of coffee a year from the highest and most expensive grades.

Currently, one shipping container of coffee beans arrives in Asia every other week to supply the company's shops. Behar said Starbucks will probably have to build a roasting plant once the number of shops in the region rises to around 100. The company has three plants in the United States.
